terms.definition: Half the diameter of a sphere — from the center to the surface. The standard way astronomers compare planet sizes.
terms.function: Lets every planet be described with one number in Earth-multiples: Mercury 0.38 ×, Earth 1 ×, Jupiter 11 ×.
terms.whereItIs: The measurement behind every label on the shelf.
terms.whyItMatters: Radius is the cleanest single number for comparing how big a world is.

terms.definition: How much space a sphere takes up; for a sphere it grows with the cube of the radius.
terms.function: Explains why Jupiter — only 11 × Earth's radius — holds more than 1,300 Earths of volume.
terms.whereItIs: Visualized by the fill toggle dropping Earth-sized spheres into Jupiter.
terms.whyItMatters: The cube jump (11 → 1,331) is why 'only 11 times wider' still means 'over a thousand times more material.'

terms.definition: A giant planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface near its clouds — Jupiter and Saturn.
terms.function: Explains why the two biggest spheres on the shelf are also the two without solid surfaces.
terms.whereItIs: The Jupiter and Saturn spheres on the shelf.
terms.whyItMatters: The largest planets are the gas giants — size and composition are linked in the solar system.

terms.definition: A round world orbiting the Sun that has not cleared its neighborhood — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea, Makemake.
terms.function: Distinguishes Pluto-sized worlds from the eight planets on the shelf.
terms.whereItIs: Not on the shelf — mentioned because learners expect Pluto there.
terms.whyItMatters: Pluto is smaller than the Moon, so it would sit below Mercury's label; that is why it is not one of the eight planets.

terms.definition: The star at the solar system's center — radius about 109 × Earth's, more than a million Earths by volume.
terms.function: Completes the size ladder behind the shelf.
terms.whereItIs: The large warm sphere floating behind the shelf.
terms.whyItMatters: The Sun holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass; its size is the scale everything else must be measured against.
